questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the survival of a document reveals
questions.stem: Planning a survey of an abandoned watermead, a biologist asks what the surviving parish papers can show.

questions.explanation: Survival is shaped twice, first by what clerks chose to record and then by what later custodians kept. The papers in hand describe the decisions of officials, not the full past they observed.

options.misconception: assumes the same marking means the same hedge

options.text: Ask whether a feature absent in 1750 and present in 1831 was new or merely unrecorded

options.misconception: treats naming frequency as a dating signal

options.text: Prefer the tithe survey, since it was made closer to the hedge in question
options.misconception: assumes later maps date features better

questions.explanation: A sound test needs a fixed question and a check on how each document was made. A feature absent in 1750 and present in 1831 dates the gap only if absence in 1750 means unrecorded, not nonexistent.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two counts of one flock disagree
questions.stem: A 1784 estate inventory counts 46 breeding ewes while a 1790 valuation counts 120 sheep, and a biologist must explain the difference in a survey report.

answer.exemplar: The two counts answer different questions about the same flock. The inventory counted animals the owner kept for breeding on the home farm, while the valuation counted every sheep on the holding for the purposes of assessment, including wethers and lambs. Neither number is wrong, and neither can be used as a check on the other, because the categories behind them differ. The report should state the definition behind each figure before any trend in flock size is described.

questions.explanation: The same flock counted for breeding and for valuation gives different totals because the categories differ. Neither figure corrects the other, so each must be reported with the question behind it.
questions.hint: Ask what each count was counting.

options.misconception: prefers the age of the witness over the record

options.misconception: accepts a secondhand judgement as verification

questions.explanation: A recollection gathered decades later is evidence of how the event was remembered, not of the count itself. It may suggest where the tally went wrong, but it cannot replace the tally.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a pamphlet about grazing can prove
questions.stem: For a survey report on common grazing, a biologist must explain what an 1837 pamphlet can establish.

answer.exemplar: A pamphlet is a piece of persuasion addressed to readers, so it can establish what someone argued, when, and to what end. The 1837 complaint about common grazing shows that a quarrel existed and reveals the writer's view of who owed what, but it cannot establish the number of sheep on the common, the dates of enclosure, or what the practice had actually been in earlier decades. The report should cite it as evidence of the dispute and use the enclosure records for the grazing itself.

questions.explanation: A pamphlet establishes that a claim was made and why, not that the claim was true. It carries the writer's account of grazing, but the extent and dates need the enclosure records.
questions.hint: It proves the argument, not the grazing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what missing records do and do not show
questions.stem: Writing up the estuary, a biologist must explain why no early fishery records survive.

answer.exemplar: The absence of fishery records is a fact about the archive, not about the estuary. Fishing was small, seasonal and often informal, so it generated little paper, and the papers that once existed were the ones most likely to be pulped, lost or ignored. The correct conclusion is a gap in the documentation, not a gap in the practice. The report should say that fishing is unrecorded before a certain date, name the record types searched, and set out the physical traces a field survey could still use, such as boat slips, nets and the shell middens along the shore.

questions.explanation: A gap in the archive is a gap in documentation, not in the activity. Fishing left little paper, so the report must describe the missing evidence and the traces a field survey can still look for.
questions.hint: Name the gap and the traces you can still use.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a test of a dating
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a dating test should be designed
questions.stem: Before designing a test for a ploughed strip, a biologist must explain how the test should be set up.

answer.exemplar: A dating test needs a feature that both makers would have recorded had it existed, and a rule for reading gaps that is fixed before the documents are opened. The biologist should first ask what each map was for, since an estate map and a tithe survey draw different features, then choose a feature both would have shown, such as a boundary hedge or a drove road. Only then does an absence in the earlier document carry meaning. The report should record the rule in advance so that the result is not chosen after the fact, and should note what the test cannot distinguish, for instance a new hedge from an old one that was coppiced.

questions.explanation: A dating test needs a fixed rule set before the documents are read, and a feature the makers would have shown. Choosing the feature after seeing the maps lets the biologist fit the rule to the result.
questions.hint: Choose the feature and the rule first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a doubled liability without calling it an error
questions.stem: In a survey report on taxation, a biologist must explain why two men are liable for one hearth.

answer.exemplar: A hearth charged twice is not necessarily a mistake, and the biologist should resist reading it as one. Tax lists often attached liability to the householder by law while another roll, made for a different levy, attached it to whoever was actually keeping the hearth in work. If that is what has happened, the double entry records two systems of responsibility rather than one hearth being counted twice. The report should set out the basis of each list, note the single household behind the two names, and avoid inflating the number of hearths in the settlement.

questions.explanation: Two names against one hearth reflects two bases of liability, such as householder and working tenant. The report should identify the basis of each list before treating the double entry as an anomaly.
questions.hint: Compare who each list makes liable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why counts in different units cannot be compared
questions.stem: A biologist must explain in a survey report why a 1685 survey of 6 bee houses and a 1701 return of 22 stocks of bees cannot be compared.

answer.exemplar: The two documents count different things, and the difference is a difference of unit rather than of fact. A bee house is a structure and a stock of bees is a living population, so one record describes where colonies were kept and the other describes how many colonies existed. Either number would be changed by the loss of a single winter, and the difference between six and twenty-two could reflect a change in method rather than in the bees. The report should state the unit behind each figure and refuse to build a trend on a change of counting practice.

questions.explanation: One count is of structures and the other of colonies, so the two are not the same measure. A change in counting practice can look like a change in the bees, and the report must say which it has.
questions.hint: Ask what unit each figure counts.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a pamphlet on drainage can show
questions.stem: For the final section, a biologist must explain what a pamphlet about enclosures can and cannot tell a reader.

answer.exemplar: A pamphlet is a claim made in public on a known date, and that is exactly what it establishes: the terms of the argument, the identity of the speaker, the grievance as it was understood and the moment at which the writer thought publication necessary. Everything else it seems to offer belongs to other records. The acreage of enclosure and the compensation paid appear in the award and the enclosure commissioners' papers; the number of households displaced appears in the tithes and the poor law records; the later condition of the open fields appears in surveys and farm accounts. A good report will use the pamphlet for the argument and send the reader elsewhere for the arithmetic.

questions.explanation: A pamphlet establishes the argument its author made at a date, and the terms in which enclosure was then discussed. It cannot settle how much land was enclosed or who was displaced.
questions.hint: Use it for the argument, not the acreage.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a silent archive still leaves a site worth survey
questions.stem: For a wood with no documentary history, a biologist must explain why it is not thereby uninteresting.

answer.exemplar: The absence of a documentary history is a statement about the archive, and it says nothing whatever about the ground. Medieval woods were exploited by people who kept few records, and what was written was often destroyed; the file of a wood can be thin precisely because the wood was valuable, since timber rights were fought over in ways that leave letters rather than accounts. The report should describe the wood on its own terms, note the documentary silence as a feature of the region rather than of the site, and use the tree rings, the pollards and the species present to carry the history the papers lack.

questions.explanation: A wood without papers may be one that generated few records or whose records were lost. The report should describe the site on its own evidence and treat the silence as a fact about the archive.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a test of a dating
questions.learningObjective: Choose features that both documents were obliged to record
questions.stem: To date a woodland enclosure, a biologist must choose a feature both tithe maps were obliged to record.

answer.exemplar: The test works only if both maps would have shown the feature, so the choice of feature has to follow the documents rather than the wish of the survey. A tithe survey was required to record certain holdings and boundaries, and an enclosure map was required to show parcels, but a feature outside either obligation tells the biologist nothing when it is missing from one of them. The report should therefore name the obligation that required the feature to be drawn, and should state plainly that the test is bounded by those obligations. Where the two maps record the feature differently, that difference is itself evidence about the land, but it is not evidence about its date, and the report should keep the two apart.

questions.explanation: The test works only if both maps would have shown the feature, so the biologist must choose one the tithe rules covered. Total woodland area.
questions.hint: Pick a feature both maps had to record.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why two returns on one manor differ
questions.stem: A 1762 land tax and a 1769 parliamentary schedule on one manor are compared by a biologist who must explain the disagreement.

answer.exemplar: Two returns on one manor were made for two different purposes, and each was shaped by what the state needed that year. The land tax was a working assessment, with its own rates, exemptions and definitions of what counted as land. The parliamentary schedule was a different exercise, often compiled for a different authority and with a different unit of account. Where they disagree, the biologist should first ask what each was counting and for whom, then treat the difference as a difference between two administrative viewpoints rather than as a contradiction in the facts of the manor.

questions.explanation: Returns on the same manor answer the year's needs, and those needs change between levies. Reading each against its own purpose is the only way to judge whether a difference is administrative or real.
questions.hint: Read each return against the year's need.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A census as an administrative act
questions.learningObjective: Judge what a commissioners' circular requires towns to count

stimulus.body: Circular of the commissioners of poor law, 1841, sent to each overseer. The commissioners require a return of the names of all persons receiving relief in each township, together with a separate statement of the number of other persons resident, distinguishing those of the age of fourteen and upwards from those below it.

questions.stem: A biologist reads a 1841 commissioners' circular and must judge what it makes the returns count.

options.text: A census of every person in the township, whatever the commissioners needed
options.misconception: reads a government order as a complete enumeration

options.text: A count of the destitute only, since relief is what the order mentions first
options.misconception: takes the first clause as the whole order

options.text: A count split between those on relief and those of working age
A record of everyone aged over fourteen, with no interest in the rest
options.misconception: mistakes an age threshold for the total population

questions.explanation: The circular defines what each township had to report: names on relief, a number of others, and those divided by age. That structure tells the biologist what the totals cover.
questions.hint: Read what the order asks each place to report.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Pair a pamphlet's argument with the records of fact
questions.stem: A biologist must decide how a pamphlet on enclosure belongs in the final section of the report.

options.text: By citing the pamphlet for the acreage, since it is the most detailed description available
options.misconception: treats a popular account as a measured record

options.text: By treating it as the last word on enclosure, since it was written for the public
options.misconception: gives a popular work the last word on fact

options.text: By ignoring it, because pamphlets were written to sell rather than to inform
options.misconception: rules out a genre because of its motive

options.text: By using it to date the argument and the award to establish the facts

questions.explanation: A pamphlet is dated evidence of a public argument, valuable for the history of opinion and useless for acreage. Pairing it with the award lets the report carry the claim and the fact together.
questions.hint: Use it for the argument, not the acreage.
